c.tagline: Laid-back BVI capital and sailing mecca, gateway to Virgin Gorda and The Baths.

taxi.fareNote: There is no Uber in the BVI — taxis are the only ride option and run on government-set fixed rates (often charged per person rather than per trip), so confirm the price before you get in.

emergency.note: Both 999 (UK-style) and 911 connect to police, fire, and ambulance across the British Virgin Islands.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

hood_landmark.Wickhams Cay 2 (The Moorings): The Moorings marina Road Town Tortola

avoid.reason: Petty theft from moored boats, rental cars and unattended beach bags occurs; skip quiet unlit back streets late at night.

hood_desc: The reclaimed marina district at the town's heart, packed with charter-yacht bases, the ferry terminal, dockside bars like Pusser's, restaurants, and shops; the natural base for sailors and first-timers.
Road Town's historic spine of pastel colonial buildings, boutiques, craft shops, the old market, and cafes running back from the harbour; the sightseeing and shopping core.
The harbourfront strip along Waterfront Drive beneath the 17th-century Fort Burt, with hillside hotels, the cruise pier, and sweeping views over Road Harbour and the Sir Francis Drake Channel.
The quieter second marina peninsula, home to The Moorings charter base and yachting hotels, a short walk from the centre but calmer and waterside.
A relaxed residential and marina area southwest of the centre around Sea Cows Bay and Nanny Cay, with a boatyard, beach, and self-contained resort feel away from the bustle.

water.note: Supply is desalinated or cistern-collected and inconsistent; most visitors drink bottled.

transit.hours: Open-air 'safari' taxis run mainly in daytime; ferries between islands run roughly 6:00 AM to early evening, with fewer sailings on Sundays.
transit.note: Road Town has no formal bus network. Getting around means open-air 'safari' taxis (shared trucks with bench seats), private taxis, and the inter-island ferries that fan out from the town's ferry terminal.
transit.pay: Taxis are cash (US dollars) at fixed government rates; ferries are paid at the terminal by cash or card. Bring small bills for safari taxis.

food.name: Fish and fungi
food.desc: The BVI national dish: cornmeal-and-okra fungi served with stewed or steamed local fish in a tomato-and-onion creole gravy.

places.name: The Dove Restaurant
places.note: Long-running Road Town favorite pairing island staples with a polished dining room.

places.name: Village Cay Restaurant
places.note: Marina-side kitchen known for local-catch plates and West Indian daily specials.

places.name: Crafts Alive Village food vendors
places.note: Local cooks sell home-style fungi plates beside the craft market stalls.

food.name: Conch fritters
food.desc: Chopped queen conch folded into a peppery batter and fried into golden bites, served with a tangy island dipping sauce.

places.name: Pusser's Road Town Pub
places.note: Harborfront institution; fritters and Painkillers are the classic combination.

places.name: Peg Legs Landing
places.note: Beachside marina bar with a well-reviewed conch and seafood starter list.

places.name: Village Cay Restaurant
places.note: Dockside spot where fritters come straight off a busy lunchtime fryer.

food.name: Roti
food.desc: Trinidad-style flatbread wrapped around curried chicken, goat, beef or conch with potato, a legacy of the islands' Indo-Caribbean cooks.

places.name: Roti Palace
places.note: Tiny upstairs kitchen that has been Tortola's go-to roti stop for decades.

places.name: Omar's Sandspit
places.note: Reopened in 2025; curries and rotis widely rated the best on the island.

places.name: Midtown Restaurant
places.note: Cash-only local diner with curries, rotis and hearty daily plates.

food.name: Pates
food.desc: Crisp fried turnovers stuffed with seasoned saltfish, chicken, beef, conch or lobster; the classic Tortolian breakfast and street snack.

places.name: Crandall's Pastry Plus
places.note: The island's best-known pate bakery; get there early, the fish pate sells out.

places.name: Crafts Alive Village food vendors

places.name: Midtown Restaurant
places.note: Reliable in-town counter for pates and other quick local bites.

food.name: Johnny cakes
food.desc: Puffy fried dough rounds split and filled with saltfish, cheese or corned beef, eaten all day long across the territory.

places.name: Crandall's Pastry Plus
places.note: Locals queue here first thing for johnny cakes hot from the fryer.

places.name: Crafts Alive Village food vendors

places.note: Serves johnny cakes as a side with local breakfast and lunch plates.

food.name: Grilled Caribbean lobster and fresh catch
food.desc: Spiny lobster and reef fish split, seasoned and grilled over coals, usually with peas and rice, plantain and a lime-butter sauce.

places.name: Le Cabanon
places.note: French-Caribbean kitchen doing careful things with the day's local catch.

places.name: Peg Legs Landing

places.name: Omar's Sandspit

food.name: Painkiller
food.desc: The BVI's own cocktail: dark navy rum shaken with pineapple and orange juice and cream of coconut, dusted with fresh nutmeg.

places.name: Pusser's Road Town Pub

food.desc: Pot-stilled rum pressed from local sugar cane at a stone distillery working since the 1700s, sold young and fiercely aromatic.

landmarks: Main Street
Road Town's historic spine of pastel wooden and stone buildings, where island shops, churches and rum-soaked history pack a photogenic Caribbean streetscape.
J.R. O'Neal Botanic Gardens
A lush four-acre oasis of orchids, palms and a pergola walk, offering shady respite and birdlife in the middle of the capital.
Old Government House Museum
The elegant former governor's residence on a harbour-view rise, restored with period furnishings, stamps and exhibits on British Virgin Islands history.
Sage Mountain National Park
Tortola's highest point at 523 metres, where trails wind through elephant-ear ferns and remnant rainforest to sweeping views over the island chain.
Cane Garden Bay
Tortola's most celebrated crescent of white sand and calm turquoise water, backed by beach bars famed for live music and painkiller cocktails.
Callwood Rum Distillery
A 400-year-old stone distillery at Cane Garden Bay still producing arawak rum by traditional methods, one of the Caribbean's oldest continuously operating distilleries.
Crafts Alive Village
A cluster of brightly painted Caribbean-style huts on the waterfront where local artisans sell straw work, batik, hot sauces and island crafts.
Fort Burt
The remains of a 17th-century Dutch-then-English fort above the harbour entrance, its old powder magazine now paired with sunset views over Road Harbour.
1780 Lower Estate Sugar Works Museum
A restored brick-and-stone sugar factory recounting Tortola's plantation era with artefacts, machinery and exhibits on emancipation and island life.
Fort George
A ruined colonial-era fort on a hilltop above Baugher's Bay, its cannon emplacements overlooking Road Town's harbor and the channel toward Peter Island.

train.note: There is no railway in the British Virgin Islands. Arrive by air into Terrance B. Lettsome airport on Beef Island, connected to Tortola by bridge, or by ferry from St Thomas and Puerto Rico.

bus.note: No international coaches - the BVI is an island group. Tortola has open-air safari buses and shared taxis that run between Road Town, West End and the beaches, mostly meeting cruise ships and ferries rather than following a fixed timetable. Car hire is common; driving is on the left.

ferry.note: Ferries are the backbone of travel here. The crossings to the US Virgin Islands are proper international sailings with immigration at both ends - carry your passport, and note that US entry requirements apply. Inter-island boats to Virgin Gorda and Jost Van Dyke run several times a day from Road Town and West End. Schedules are cut back on Sundays and change seasonally, so check the day before.
